newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.S. stevedore Ceres to boost Amsterdam containers.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stevedore Ceres to boost Amsterdam containers.

text.p: U.S. stevedore Ceres has agreed a major investment in Amsterdam, completing the purchase of CTA group and announcing plans for a new terminal that will sharply boost the port's container capacity, officials said on Monday.
Around 65,000 20-foot containers pass through CTA terminals each year, and Ceres plans to raise this initially to around 120,000.
The new terminal -- a 125-acre site in the Amerikahaven -- will be able to handle several hundred thousand containers annually when completed.

"More and more goods are being shipped in containers. This sector is a growth market which Amsterdam will surely make use of and for which its port now offers good facilities," Godfried van den Heuvel, the port's executive director, said.

Chicago-based Ceres is owned by Greek-American businessman Christos Kritikos and was established in the late 1950s. It operates 15 terminals in the U.S. and Canada and handled 1.3 million containers in 1995.

Its agreement with the port authority to purchase the troubled Combined Terminals Amsterdam (CTA) marks the latest twist in the tale of the Dutch stevedore, which was originally owned by transport firms Nedlloyd and Internatio-Mueller but went into receivership in 1995.
In addition to taking over CTA's operations, Ceres has agreed to develop the new terminal.
The port authority is supplying 100 million guilders and Ceres the remaining 50 million. Financial details of the purchase of CTA were not disclosed.

In a separate move on Monday, Nedlloyd and Britain's Peninsular and Oriental Steam Navigation Co Plc (P&O), said they would merge their container businesses, creating one of the world's largest companies in the sector.
A spokeswoman for the port said it was too early to say if Amsterdam would accrue any benefit from that deal. But she added any general growth in container traffic would be beneficial.
"All sorts of cargo is being shipped in containers. In particular for Amsterdam, this means cocoa beans," she said.
The city's cocoa processors are the largest in Europe, grinding nearly 400,000 tonnes of beans a year of mostly African origin into products for use in chocolate manufacture.

The trade has traditionally shipped beans in jute sacks but increasing competition has led to the major players looking at larger and larger quantities. Experiments this year led by U.S. trade house Cargill proved successful and the company plans to move much more of this season's African crops in containers.

The first shipments of the season are expected in November and some industry sources reckon that up to half of next year's cocoa imports could come into the country via container shipment, which offers substantial cost benefits.

Last month, the Amsterdam port authority announced half-year traffic figures of 26.9 million tonnes, up 7.3 percent on the same period in 1995, a total which included a 55 percent leap in container business to one million tonnes.
